study_identification_part.si4_title: Individualized cerebellar damage predicts the presence of behavioral disorders in children with brainstem tumors

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To investigate cerebellar damage patterns resulting from brainstem tumors in children and their association with behavioral disorders, using normative modeling to assess individual structural deviations and predict behavioral outcomes.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.answer: ACAPULCO v0.2.1 (pediatric template); MRIcroGL for brainstem VOI exclusion; ITK-SNAP for manual corrections; 26 cerebellar lobules from original 28 regions (VIIIA and VIIIB merged into VIII)
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The paper provides detailed description of the preprocessing workflow. First, brainstem was excluded using MRIcroGL to avoid misclassification. Then ACAPULCO package (version 0.2.1) with pediatric template was used for cerebellar segmentation. Quality control was performed by two neurosurgery specialists, with manual corrections using ITK-SNAP. Finally, lobules VIIIA and VIIIB were merged into single lobules VIII due to inconsistent boundaries, resulting in 26 cerebellar lobules.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: First, the brainstem was excluded to avoid misclassification by delineating it as the volume of interest (VOI) using MRIcroGL. Next, preprocessed MRI data from patients, along with data from healthy children, were then processed using the ACAPULCO package (version 0.2.1) with a pediatric template to generate segmented cerebellar images... Following this, segmentation quality was independently inspected by two neurosurgery specialists... manual corrections were performed for inaccurately segmented images based on cerebellar lobule anatomical morphology using ITK-SNAP... Due to inconsistent boundaries between lobules VIIIA and VIIIB, these regions were merged into single lobules VIII for the left and right sides, respectively. caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-score calculated from GPR normative model; extreme deviation threshold |Z| > 1.96 (below 2.5th percentile or above 97.5th percentile); total outlier count (tOC) summed across all 26 cerebellar regions for each participant
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper clearly describes the deviation quantification approach. For each patient and cerebellar region, a Z-score was calculated based on observed vs predicted volume from the GPR model, incorporating predictive uncertainty. Outliers were identified using a threshold of Z < -1.96 (below 2.5th percentile) for volume reductions. The total outlier count (tOC) was computed by summing outliers across all 26 regions for each participant.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: For each glioma patient, we utilized normative percentile charts from healthy children to assess individual deviations in cerebellar region volumes. Deviations were quantified by computing a Z-score based on observed and predicted volume values for each region... Outliers with diminished cerebellar volume (<-1.96, below the 2.5th percentile of the normative distribution) were identified in each region. We focused on this lower threshold to assess volume reductions linked to tumors. The tOC across all 26 regions was calculated for each participant.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Pearson correlation analysis between tOC and behavioral scores (social problems, withdrawal behaviors). Ridge regression models with nested 5-fold cross-validation (5F-CV) to predict behavioral scores from tOC; 101 repetitions of 5F-CV with grid search for optimal λ parameter (2^-10 to 2^5); linear regression within each fold to adjust for age and sex effects. Permutation testing (1000 iterations) to assess significance by creating null distribution. Ridge regression models combining 26 cerebellar region volumes as feature vectors to predict behavior scores; feature weights indicate importance and direction of association for each region; significance determined through 1000 permutation tests. Multiple linear regression to explore associations between clinical variables (duration, tumor volume, KPS, location, DIPG, symptoms) and tOC. Supplementary case-control behavioral analysis between 126 patients and 72 healthy children. Two-tailed p-value threshold of 0.05 for statistical significance.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Over 95% of patients showed cerebellar volume reductions (particularly in anterior lobules), with higher total outlier counts (tOC) significantly associated with worse social problems (r=0.31, p=0.001) and withdrawal behaviors (r=0.28, p=0.001); cerebellar volume deviations predicted these behaviors (social: r=0.27, p=0.007; withdrawal: r=0.25, p=0.015), with posterior and anterior regions (lobules X, IX, VIII, V, IV) showing strongest negative associations.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study found widespread cerebellar structural abnormalities in over 95% of patients with brainstem tumors, with the most severe negative deviations in anterior lobules (Left I-V, Right I-V) and vermis (IV-VII). Total outlier count (tOC) showed significant positive correlation with tumor volume (r=0.41, p<0.001). Multiple regression analysis revealed tOC was significantly associated with social problems (p=0.046) and withdrawal behaviors (p=0.008). Pearson correlation analysis showed tOC significantly correlated with social problems (r=0.31, p=0.001) and withdrawal behaviors (r=0.28, p=0.001). Ridge regression models demonstrated that tOC could predict social problems (mean r=0.27, p=0.030) and withdrawal behaviors (mean r=0.25, p=0.034). When using cerebellar volume deviations from all 26 regions as predictors, the models achieved significant prediction accuracy for social problems (r=0.27, p=0.007) and withdrawal behaviors (r=0.25, p=0.015). Feature weight analysis revealed that reduced volumes in posterior cerebellar regions (Right X, Left X, Left IX, Left VIII, Right VIIB) and anterior regions (Right V, Left V, Right IV, Left IV) were most strongly associated with worse social problems, while Left V, Right IV, Vermis VIII, Vermis VI, and similar regions contributed most to withdrawal behavior predictions. These findings emphasize the role of both anterior and posterior cerebellar lobes in behavioral disorders in brainstem tumor patients.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The normative model included only age and gender, not accounting for education or home environment; the behavioral questionnaire focused mainly on social problems and lacked depth in assessing social functions; correlation between cerebellar deformation and behavioral disturbances does not establish causality
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Firstly, the normative model included only age and gender. It did not account for education or home environment, which might affect brain indices. Therefore, future models should include these factors. Secondly, the questionnaire focused mainly on social problems. It lacked depth in assessing social functions. A more specialized tool is needed. Thirdly, we found a correlation between cerebellar deformation and behavioral disturbances in pediatric patients. However, this does not establish causality.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study used U-Net-based ACAPULCO algorithm for automated cerebellar segmentation with pediatric template, enabling precise quantification in deformed cerebellums. Manual quality control by two independent neurosurgery specialists ensured segmentation accuracy. ComBat harmonization was applied to multi-site healthy control data while preserving biological covariates (age, sex, TIV). The tOC metric was validated as an individualized indicator of cerebellar damage. Feature weight analysis from ridge regression identified specific cerebellar lobules contributing to behavioral predictions. The study demonstrates potential for early recognition of cognitive and behavioral disorders to facilitate timely medical intervention.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study examined secondary cerebellar changes in pediatric brainstem tumor patients (n=147, age 4-17 years, mean 8.5±3.5 years) from Beijing Tiantan Hospital. The normative model was trained on 849 healthy children (age 4-18 years, mean 11.44±3.3 years) from 4 different sites. Behavioral assessment was completed for 126 of the 147 patients using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). The study excluded patients whose tumors infiltrated the cerebellum, focusing on indirect cerebellar damage from brainstem tumors. Tumor locations: pons (62.6%), multi-locations (20.4%), medulla (8.8%), midbrain (8.2%). Mean tumor volume was 26.97±14.7 cm³. Clinical symptoms included limb weakness (57.8%), ataxia (55.8%), diplopia (54.4%), bucking (44.9%), headache (28.6%), emesis (28.6%), dysarthria (25.2%), and dysphagia (16.3%). The study provides evidence for the cerebro-brainstem-cerebellar circuit's role in social behaviors and suggests that protecting cerebellar-brainstem functional circuits could be crucial for preserving patient function. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/heyuanJ/cerebellum. The study was approved by Beijing Tiantan Hospital IRB (Approval No. KY 2019-124-02) and complies with Chinese regulations on human genetic resources.
